Part 1 — Dr. Reem Alyahya (group A, taught earlier)

Introduction to Trauma

  • Trauma: Definition, Significance, and Mechanism of Injury
    • Trauma: Injury caused by external force or violence.
    • Leading cause of death, especially in people under 45 years.
    • Mechanism of Injury: Blunt, Penetrating, Thermal.
Speaker notes

• Trauma is defined as an injury caused by external force or violence. It includes a broad range of injuries, from minor cuts and bruises to severe, life-threatening conditions.

• Trauma is a significant global health issue, especially as a leading cause of death in younger populations. It's a leading cause of death in people under 45 years old.

• Understanding the mechanism of injury (blunt, penetrating, or thermal) is crucial for predicting potential internal damage and planning treatment.

Notes

Definition & Importance

DEFINITION
Trauma = injury caused by an external force/violence. Major cause of death and disability, particularly in young people — leading cause of death age 1–45 years. The major burden is not only mortality: survivors may have permanent disability. Best strategy = prevention whenever possible (e.g. road-safety measures reducing RTAs).
Notes

Types of Trauma

TypeNotes
BluntMVCs, falls, other non-penetrating mechanisms — significant internal injury/hemorrhage may exist with little or no external evidence
PenetratingStab wounds, gunshot wounds
BurnsThermal, chemical, electrical; thermal injury may include heat/cold exposure
CrushE.g. workers trapped/crushed by heavy objects
BlastCombination of penetrating fragments, burns, crush injury; injury pattern may be widespread/unpredictable
Mass-casualty events may trigger hospital-wide emergency activation with multiple specialties/teams prepared simultaneously.
  • Electrical burn + 3-m fall, unconscious → intubation. 437 ×2
Notes

Trauma Management Principles

Unlike elective disease management, trauma cannot be scheduled/planned for a specific patient. Requires rapid, accurate physiological assessment, immediate resuscitation, and the ability to stabilize and transfer if definitive treatment is unavailable locally (e.g. stabilize/intubate a spinal-trauma patient, then transfer if neurosurgical/spine services unavailable).

TEAMWORK IS ESSENTIAL
Team leader, airway/resuscitation staff, nurses, blood sampling/access personnel, transport/support personnel — an individual physician cannot manage major trauma alone.

STATESTICS

  • Leading cause of death in ages 1 through 44
  • Disabilities exceed deaths by ratio of 3:1
  • Trauma-related costs > $400 billion per year globally
  • Lack of public awareness for injury prevention
  • Leading cause of death and disability in trauma → head injury. 432 ×4
Notes

Preparation

Trauma care depends heavily on anticipation and preparation before patient arrival. Prehospital notification allows preparation of blood products, imaging, trauma team, and OR standby when major surgery is likely. Lack of preparation → delays while waiting for X-ray, technicians, radiology, OR, etc. Peripheral hospitals should at minimum be capable of initial resuscitation, stabilization, and appropriate transfer.
HEALTHCARE-WORKER PROTECTION
Use PPE/protective gowns because trauma patients may have infectious or chemical hazards.
Notes

ATLS

ATLS = Advanced Trauma Life Support. Developed after an orthopedic surgeon and his family were injured in a road accident in the 1970s and received poorly prioritized trauma care. Core idea: everyone caring for trauma patients should use the same systematic priorities, even with limited resources.
  • Most important determinant in reducing injury at impact in a road accident → speed limitation. 430
Notes

Distribution of Trauma Deaths

TimingDescription
ImmediateAt scene/within seconds–minutes; usually catastrophic injuries with little opportunity for medical intervention
EarlyWithin hours — main preventable cause: hemorrhage/blood loss. This is the golden hour, when rapid intervention can save the patient
LateAfter approximately 2–3 weeks — severely injured patients may develop overwhelming infection/sepsis after prolonged physiological and immune stress

Types of Trauma

  • Blunt Trauma: Falls, Motor Vehicle Accidents.
    • These injuries can be challenging to diagnose due to the potential for hidden damage, requiring careful monitoring and imaging
    • Penetrating Trauma: Stab Wounds, Gunshot Wounds.
    • Burns: Thermal, Chemical, Electrical.
    • Crush Injuries: body parts are compressed under heavy objects, leading to muscle damage, compartment syndrome, and potential renal failure
    • Blast Injuries: cause a combination of all types
Speaker notes

• Blunt Trauma: Common causes include falls, motor vehicle accidents, or physical assaults. Injuries can range from fractures and internal bleeding to organ lacerations and traumatic brain injuries. These injuries can be challenging to diagnose due to the potential for hidden damage, requiring careful monitoring and imaging.

• Penetrating Trauma: Often results from stab wounds, gunshot wounds, or impalement. These injuries involve direct damage to organs, blood vessels, and tissues, with a high risk of infection and hemorrhage. Penetrating injuries are typically easier to identify but are often more severe, requiring immediate imaging and possibly surgery.

• Burns: Can be thermal, chemical, or electrical in nature. Discussing the extent of burns, such as using the rule of nines to estimate burn surface area, is important.

• Crush Injuries: These occur when body parts are compressed under heavy objects, leading to muscle damage, compartment syndrome, and potential renal failure.

• Blast Injuries: Result from explosions and can cause a combination of blunt and penetrating trauma, as well as burns and potential inhalation injuries.

Goals/ Principles of Trauma Care

ALTS

"When I can provide better care in the field with limited resources than what my children and I received at the primary care facility, there is something wrong with the system and the system has to be changed”

  • James K. Styner 1972
  • orthopedic surgeon, crashed his plane.
  • His wife was killed instantly
  • three of his four children sustained critical injuries. He carried out the initial triage of his children at the crash site.
  • transport him to the nearest hospital; where they were treated was inadequate and inappropriate.

Trimodal Death Distribution

Primary Survey: ABCDE

  • Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS)
    • A: Airway and cervical spine control.
    • B: Breathing and ventilation.
    • C: Circulation
    • D: Disability (neurological status).
    • E: Exposure and environmental control.
Speaker notes

• The ABCDE approach is a systematic way to assess and manage trauma patients in life-threatening situations. It helps ensure that no critical steps are missed.

• A - Airway with Cervical Spine Control: Ensuring the airway is clear and protecting the cervical spine are critical. Techniques like jaw-thrust or chin-lift maneuvers can be used, and intubation may be necessary if the airway is compromised. Signs of airway obstruction include stridor and hoarseness.

• B - Breathing and Ventilation: Assess breathing by observing chest rise, listening to breath sounds, and checking oxygen saturation. Identify life-threatening conditions such as tension pneumothorax, hemothorax, or flail chest. Management may include needle decompression, chest tube insertion, or positive pressure ventilation.

• C - Circulation with Hemorrhage Control: Check for signs of shock, including hypotension, tachycardia, and weak pulses. Control external bleeding with direct pressure, tourniquets, or hemostatic agents. Initiate fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids or blood products.

• D - Disability (Neurological Status): Quickly assess neurological status using the AVPU scale (Alert, Verbal response, Pain response, Unresponsive) or Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). Look for signs of head injury, increased intracranial pressure, or spinal cord injury.

• E - Exposure and Environmental Control: Fully expose the patient to assess for additional injuries while preventing hypothermia. Use warm blankets, warmed IV fluids, and manage the environment to prevent further heat loss.

GCS ≤ 8 → intubate (can't protect the airway). Suspected C-spine injury → jaw thrust (no head tilt), in-line immobilization while securing the airway.
  • Trachea to the left, right chest hyperresonant → needle decompression, 2nd ICS MCL, right side 442; agitated, hypotensive after MVA → needle decompression 434 ×2 430 431; site → 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line 436 ×4; irrelevant in tension pneumothorax → "confirm chest-tube position with CT". 438
  • Chest tube site → 4th–5th ICS (above the 5th rib), mid-axillary line — level of the nipple, in the safe triangle 437 ×2 427 435; inserted with full aseptic technique 436; not an indication → pneumoperitoneum. 437
  • Fluid of choice → isotonic crystalloid — keyed 0.9% saline in one recall, Ringer's lactate in others 442 441 434 ×2 431 ×3 430; crush/extraction → 1 L Ringer's bolus. 438 ×7
  • GCS = best eye, verbal and motor responses 430 ×3; no eye opening (1) + incomprehensible sounds (2) + extension (2) → 5 437 ×4; eyes to pain (2) + sounds (2) + flexion (3) → 7 431 ×2; eyes to voice (3) + confused (4) + obeys (6) → 13. 426
Notes

Primary Survey — ABCDE

UNIVERSAL TRAUMA LANGUAGE
A — Airway + cervical spine protection B — Breathing/ventilation
C — Circulation + hemorrhage control D — Disability / neurological assessment E — Exposure + environmental control
PRINCIPLE
Save life before limb. Do not focus on a limb fracture while the patient is hypoxic, hypotensive, or actively bleeding. Assessment occurs rapidly and often simultaneously within the team, but priorities remain A → B → C → D → E.
  • Aim of the primary survey → identify (and treat) life-threatening injuries 441; condition primarily assessed and managed in it → hypoxia 442; correct order → airway with c-spine, breathing, circulation. 430
Notes

A — Airway + Cervical Spine Protection

Airway Assessment

Simplest initial test: Can the patient speak? Speaking normally → airway is currently patent. Unconscious/non-responsive patient may not protect the airway. Inspect for secretions/blood (suction if needed), foreign body, gurgling/abnormal sounds, obstruction.

  • Agitated, bloody secretions in the mouth, respiratory distress, bleeding femur → first suction the mouth (rigid catheter) 438 ×5; raccoon eyes with nasal bleeding → immediate threat airway obstruction. 429 ×2
Notes

Definitive Airway

Definitive airway = endotracheal tube passed through the vocal cords with an inflated protective cuff — provides a secure airway and delivers ventilation directly into the trachea. An oxygen mask or supraglottic airway such as an LMA does NOT constitute a definitive airway, since it does not pass through the vocal cords.
  • Haematemesis — first step → airway (ensure/secure it) 438 ×5 438 ×3
Notes

Cervical Spine

Airway assessment always includes cervical spine protection. The cervical spine is mobile and potentially vulnerable in trauma; missed injury may lead to severe neurological deficit/paralysis. Protect initially even if injury has not yet been proven — apply cervical immobilization/C-collar until cervical injury has been appropriately excluded.

Airway

  • Assess for airway patency
  • Snoring, Gurgling, Stridor
  • Maxillofacial trauma/ laryngeal injury
  • Chin lift/ Modified jaw thrust
  • Look, listen, feel for chest wall motion
  • Remove particulate matter
  • Definitive airway as necessary
  • Snoring unresponsive footballer / maxillofacial fracture → open the airway with a jaw thrust 432 ×3 432 438 ×3; fall from height, needs airway → in-line immobilization and a definitive airway. 438 ×6

Breathing

  • Inspect for Chest rise and symmetry
  • Palpate
  • Percussion
  • Auscultation for breath sounds
  • O2 saturation
  • Rate/ Effort
  • Color/ Sensorium
  • Unrestrained driver — key breathing finding → breath sounds. 438 ×3
Notes

B — Breathing & Ventilation

A patent airway does not guarantee adequate ventilation/oxygenation. Assessment: inspect, palpate, percuss, auscultate, check oxygen saturation.

StepFindings
InspectionSymmetrical chest movement, reduced/absent movement on one side, stab wound/open injury, visible thoracic trauma, paradoxical chest movement
PalpationRib fractures/crepitus, subcutaneous (surgical) emphysema (air under the skin, crackling/bubble-wrap sensation)
PercussionHyperresonance → pneumothorax; dullness → fluid/solid material (e.g. hemothorax)
AuscultationReduced/absent air entry may be the first clue to major thoracic injury
SUBCUTANEOUS EMPHYSEMA
Suspect injury to the respiratory tract, especially pneumothorax, tracheal, or bronchial injury. In trauma: pneumothorax until proven otherwise. Combined findings of asymmetric chest movement + hyperresonance + absent air entry support pneumothorax. If tension pneumothorax is suspected → act immediately; do not delay lifesaving management.
  • Tracheal deviation, hyperresonance/absent breath sounds, hypotension → tension pneumothorax 439 437 — an obstructive shock 442 434; after a subclavian line → tension pneumothorax. 438 ×3
  • Flail chest — the false statement → "managed by thoracotomy" (analgesia, oxygen, ventilation if needed). 427
  • Stab to the neck, stable, subcutaneous emphysema + expanding haematoma (hard signs) → emergency neck exploration. 439 ×2
Notes

Oxygenation

SpO₂ is connected early as part of trauma monitoring. A speaking patient with SpO₂ >90% is relatively reassuring. Markedly low saturation (e.g. <80%) requires immediate correction before moving to less urgent examination.

TIME-CRITICAL
Brain injury can occur within only a few minutes of severe hypoxia — ~4 minutes without oxygen was emphasized.

Circulation

  • Heart rate
  • Blood pressure
  • Assess organ perfusion
    • Level of consciousness
    • Skin color
    • Pulse rate and character
  • Look for blood in: chest, abdomen, long bone and blood on the floor

Hypotension in trauma is

hemorrhagic shock until

proven otherwise

  • Analgesia in a shocked polytrauma patient → IV (poor absorption from muscle/skin in shock). 438 ×7
Notes

C — Circulation & Hemorrhage

Assess: heart rate, blood pressure, level of consciousness, skin color, pulse rate and character, overall organ perfusion.

CLINICAL PERFUSION
A patient who is sitting, awake, and talking has adequate cerebral perfusion at that moment — physiologically this suggests systolic pressure is likely around ≥90 mmHg, even if monitors are unavailable. Deteriorating consciousness may be an early sign of falling perfusion.

Features suggesting blood loss: tachycardia, hypotension, pallor, altered consciousness, weak pulse.

IAP ≥ 25 mmHg with new organ dysfunction, or IAH refractory to medical management → surgical decompression.
Notes

Where Can a Trauma Patient Bleed?

SiteNotes
Blood on the floorExternal hemorrhage
ChestHemothorax — one hemithorax may contain up to ~2 L
Abdomen/pelvisMay accommodate approximately 3–4 L
Retroperitoneum/pelvis—
Long bones (esp. femur)One femoral fracture may hide ~1.5–2 L; bilateral femoral fractures alone may produce severe/Class III shock
Even humeral or other long-bone fractures can contribute clinically significant blood loss.
Notes

⭐ Most Important Trauma Rule

CORE RULE
In a trauma patient, hypotension/hypoperfusion = hemorrhage until proven otherwise.

Trauma hypotension has other possible causes: obstructive shock, cardiogenic shock, neurogenic shock, septic shock, etc. Neurogenic shock may produce hypotension + bradycardia. Nevertheless, during the golden hour, initially manage the hypotensive trauma patient as hemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise — prepare blood/resuscitation and actively search for bleeding rather than delaying while considering many alternative diagnoses. If another cause is later identified, management can then be adjusted.

Hemorrhagic shock = most important preventable cause of early trauma death.

Hemorrhagic shock

  • is the most common cause of death in the fist hour of trauma
  • Be careful: elderly, pregnant, medications and athlete
  • If there is a bleeder -> STOP IT
    • Apply pressure
    • Go to OR
Hypotension in trauma is haemorrhagic shock until proven otherwise. Haemorrhagic shock is the most common cause of death in the first hour. If there is a bleeder → STOP IT (pressure, OR). Beware: elderly, pregnant, medications (β-blockers), athletes.
Notes

Hemorrhagic Shock Classification

Approximate adult circulating blood volume = 5–6 L.

ClassBlood LossKey Features
I<~1 LPhysiological compensation usually maintains normal vital signs; earliest/minimal change may be anxiety
II~1 L or moreHR begins to exceed ~100/min; BP may still remain normal (compensation); pulse pressure may begin to change; urine output begins to decrease; patient generally remains awake/conscious
IIIMore significantMarked tachycardia; HR may reach ~120–130/min or more. Bilateral major femoral fractures alone may reach this stage
IVExtremeImmediate life-threatening emergency; patient may be close to cardiovascular collapse/death
SPECIAL POPULATIONS
Elderly, children, pregnancy, and patients taking medications such as beta-blockers may not follow the usual vital-sign pattern.
  • Tachycardic with normal BP after an RTA → class II 430; what the shock class reflects → the amount of intravascular volume loss. 431
  • Pregnant woman with a large bleed yet stable → her increased stroke volume (cardiac output and blood volume ↑) 442; another version keyed increased heart rate. 437
Notes

Immediate Hemorrhage Control

ABCDE does not mean ignoring obvious catastrophic external hemorrhage. If active bleeding is visible → stop it immediately. Methods: direct pressure, tourniquet when appropriate, operative hemorrhage control.

EXAMPLE
BP 80/60, HR 120, ultrasound shows intra-abdominal bleeding → do not continue leisurely through D/E or secondary survey. Resuscitate and take patient to OR to stop bleeding.
If the patient is stuck at C because hemorrhage is uncontrolled, do not progress until C is controlled.

Disability

  • Baseline neurologic evaluation
  • Glasco coma scale
Notes

Duration of the Primary Survey

The primary survey does not necessarily finish within minutes in severely unstable trauma — e.g. patient actively bleeding → OR for packing → ICU resuscitation → return to OR later. The primary survey remains incomplete until major life-threatening ABC problems are controlled; detailed neurological/other examination may therefore be delayed.

Save life before limb. Priorities stay A → B → C → D → E; the primary survey identifies and treats life-threatening problems and stays "open" until ABC is controlled.
  • Massive transfusion complications → citrate toxicity (hypocalcaemia) 431 ×3 426; hyperkalaemia 431 ×2; ABO-incompatible transfusion → acute haemolytic reaction. 431 ×2
Notes

D — Disability

Rapid neurological assessment: baseline neurological status, ability to move limbs, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS).

GCS
Minimum possible GCS = 3 (GCS 2 is impossible, even in a dead/unresponsive patient). Moderate head injury: GCS 9–12. Severe head injury: GCS 3–8. GCS ≤8 indicates severe impairment/unconsciousness and inability to reliably protect the airway. Mild head injury occupies the higher GCS range.

If screening reveals neurological deficit → perform more detailed neurological evaluation once immediate threats are controlled.

  • Severe maxillofacial injury, can't intubate → cricothyroidotomy 432 ×5; unconscious stabbed man → endotracheal intubation 432 ×4; GCS 7 / GCS 6 → intubate. 439 431

Exposure

  • Completely undress the patient
  • Remove helmet if present
  • Look for visible / palpable injuries
  • Log roll, protect spine
  • Prevent hypothermia
Notes

E — Exposure & Environmental Control

Completely undress/expose the seriously injured patient to identify hidden injuries — examine anterior and posterior body. Cut clothing if necessary in emergencies. Remove helmets using appropriate technique while maintaining C-spine protection. Look and palpate for injuries.

  • Access: two large-bore IV lines 431; difficult peripheral access → intraosseous 432 ×2; venous cut-down → long saphenous vein anterior to the medial malleolus. 436 ×2 427
Notes

Log Roll

Log rolling allows examination of the back while maintaining spinal alignment — important because significant wounds/bleeding may be hidden posteriorly. Part of the primary survey in local practice.
Notes

Prevent Hypothermia

After exposure: cover and warm the patient. Important for privacy but especially to prevent hypothermia — hypovolemic/hemorrhagic patients are particularly vulnerable.

Urine output reflects renal perfusion but should not be the sole immediate marker during early resuscitation.
  • Best guide to resuscitation → urine output 434 ×5 431 ×3; marker of occult hypoperfusion → lactate 438 ×2; MAP for 80/50 → 60. 438 ×2
Notes

FAST

FAST = Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma. Rapid bedside ultrasound for free fluid/internal bleeding — considered part of primary trauma assessment.

Notes

DPL

DPL = Diagnostic Peritoneal Lavage. Older investigation; now rarely required because ultrasound/CT are widely available, but historically useful where imaging is unavailable. Technique: small abdominal entry, instill approximately 1 L saline, aspirate fluid and assess for evidence of intra-abdominal injury. Positive findings: gross blood, enteric/food material, elevated cell counts (WBC >500/mm³ specifically mentioned).

Secondary Survey: Start After

  • Primary survey completed
  • Resuscitation in process
  • ABCDEs reassessed
  • Vital functions returning to normal
Notes

Secondary Survey

WHEN TO PERFORM
Only when the primary survey is completed sufficiently, the patient has been resuscitated, and vital signs are stabilizing/normalizing. Unstable patient → no secondary survey; continue resuscitation and definitive control of life-threatening injury.

Secondary Survey

  • Comprehensive Head-to-Toe Examination:
    • Detailed physical examination for all injuries
    • AMPLE History:
      • Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last meal, Events.
  • Transfer patient if needed
Speaker notes

• After the primary survey and initial stabilization, conduct a thorough head-to-toe examination to identify all injuries, including those that may not be immediately life-threatening.

• The AMPLE history (Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events leading to the injury) is important to gather information that can influence treatment decisions, such as potential drug interactions, surgical considerations, and understanding the mechanism of injury.

  • Drug proven to reduce trauma mortality → tranexamic acid (within 3 h). 432 ×2
Notes

Components

Detailed head-to-toe examination to detect less immediately life-threatening injuries, including small extremity/finger/toe/ear injuries that may otherwise be missed. Full trauma history using AMPLE.

Notes

AMPLE History

LetterStands For

PPast medical history
LLast meal
EEvents/environment surrounding the injury (e.g. fall from height, MVC, mechanism)
Last meal is particularly relevant if anesthesia/urgent surgery may be required. Imaging During Secondary Survey
Once sufficiently stable, additional investigations may include CT, angiography, echocardiography, other definitive imaging.
Unstable patient should not be transported to CT merely to obtain a diagnosis.

Secondary Survey: Adjuncts

  • Blood tests
  • Urinalysis
  • CT, US
  • Angiography
  • Echocardiography
  • Bronchoscopy

Tertiary survey

  • When ?
  • Full body examination
  • Necessary imaging to rule out injuries which were missed on admission
  • Must be ruled out in the primary survey → open pneumothorax 431 ×3; most often missed in the primary survey → cardiac contusion. 437
Notes

Tertiary Survey

Performed after approximately 24 hours, once the patient remains stable — essentially a repeat detailed assessment to identify missed injuries. Necessary because during initial emergency resuscitation, patient/adrenaline may mask pain, and small fractures or soft-tissue injuries may be overlooked (e.g. finger fracture discovered after major life-threatening injuries have been controlled).
  • Life-threatening vascular injury after an RTA, nobody with him → no consent needed (emergency). 438 ×2

Trauma Triad of death

CoagulopathyAcidosis

Hypothermia

Lethal triad: coagulopathy · acidosis · hypothermia.
  • "Triad of death" → acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy. 439
  • Gift: the "triad of death" → acidosis, hypothermia and coagulopathy. 439
Notes

Damage-Control Surgery

THE LETHAL TRIAD
Severely bleeding trauma patients may enter: hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy. Massive blood loss → loss/dilution of clotting factors and platelets; hypothermia and acidosis impair coagulation enzyme function. Continuing a long definitive operation may worsen physiology further.
PRINCIPLE
When lethal physiology develops → damage control rather than prolonged definitive surgery.
  • No time for cross-match → O negative 442; massive transfusion = one blood volume in 24 h 431 ×2; ratio → 1:1:1 (RBC:plasma:platelets) 442; after 6 units of packed cells → add FFP 441 ×2; in massive bleeding we ideally transfuse → whole blood. 426

Damage control

3 stages of damage control

1- OR: stop bleeding/contamination

2- ICU: resuscitate

3- Definitive treatment

Speaker notes

• The key takeaway is that a systematic approach to trauma management, using the ABCDE method, is essential for ensuring that all critical aspects are addressed.

• The Q&A session is an opportunity to clarify any doubts, discuss areas of uncertainty, and reinforce the students' understanding of trauma management.

Notes

Stage 1 — Abbreviated Operation

Do only what is necessary:

Stop hemorrhage (ligate vessel, pack bleeding areas)
Control contamination (e.g. staple/resect injured bowel and leave in discontinuity rather than performing a prolonged reconstruction)
Temporary abdominal closure may be used
Notes

Stage 2 — ICU Resuscitation

Correct physiology: blood products, coagulation factors/platelets as required, acidosis, hypothermia, hemodynamic instability.

Notes

Stage 3 — Return to OR

Once physiology improves: definitive repair/reconstruction, bowel reconstruction/anastomosis as appropriate, definitive abdominal closure.

Do not prolong surgery trying to perform perfect definitive repair while the patient is physiologically collapsing.

Notes

Special Trauma Populations

Elderly

Main problems: reduced physiological reserve — may deteriorate suddenly rather than showing gradual compensatory changes. Medications may mask shock signs.

Beta-Blockers

May prevent expected tachycardia despite significant hemorrhage — the patient may already have Class II or worse shock while appearing to have a relatively normal heart rate. Do not label an elderly trauma patient "stable" based only on normal HR/BP; review medications and maintain a high index of suspicion for occult bleeding. Outcome depends on early/aggressive recognition and management.

Children

  • Leading cause of death
  • Immature, anatomic/ mechanical features
  • Vigorous physiologic response
  • Limited physiologic reserve
  • Outcome depends on early aggressive care
Notes

Children

Smaller circulating blood volume relative to adults — even a seemingly small absolute blood loss may represent a major percentage of total blood volume. Children have strong physiological compensation and may maintain apparently normal vital signs despite substantial hemorrhage. Once compensation fails → can crash rapidly. Significant shock can be present before obvious hypotension appears.

Pregnancy

  • Anatomic/ physiologic changes modify response to injury
  • Need for fetal assessment
  • 1st Priority: Maternal resuscitation
  • Outcome depends on early, aggressive care
  • Gestation and position of uterus
  • Physiologic anemia
  • ↓ Pco2
  • ↓ Gastric emptying
  • Supine hypotension
Notes

Pregnancy

PRIORITY — MOTHER FIRST
Major determinant/leading cause of fetal death in trauma = maternal death. Saving/stabilizing the mother provides the best chance of saving the fetus. Family preference does not override the medical priority of maternal resuscitation.

Imaging: if CT is medically required for maternal trauma evaluation → perform CT despite pregnancy; do not withhold lifesaving imaging because of fetal concerns. Once maternal resuscitation is underway/stable → perform appropriate fetal assessment.

PHYSIOLOGICAL CONSIDERATIONS
Supine hypotension: enlarged uterus may compress the IVC when the patient lies flat — use left lateral tilt/positioning to reduce compression. Physiological anemia occurs in pregnancy. Increased ventilation lowers CO₂ → mild respiratory alkalosis may be normal.
  • Third-trimester trauma on a spine board → tilt to the left (relieve aortocaval compression). 439

Examples

Tension

pneumothorax

Notes

Tension Pneumothorax Example

Chest X-ray findings: loss of normal lung markings on affected side, tracheal/mediastinal shift — consistent with tension pneumothorax.

Clinically, suspected tension pneumothorax is a rapidly fatal B problem and requires immediate action rather than delaying treatment for extensive investigation.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis — decompress immediately, no X-ray first. Needle in the 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line (ATLS 10 now advises the 4th–5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary line in adults), then a chest tube.

Abdominal trauma Spleen

  • The most injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma
  • Signs and symptoms
    • abdominal pain, tenderness in the epigastrium and left flank.
    • Kehr's sign: sharp pain in the left shoulder
    • hypovolemic shock
  • Diagnosis
    • FAST: if patient is unstable go to OR
    • CTL if patient is stable
  • Most injured organ in blunt abdominal trauma → spleen 442 ×2 442 ×2; car crash on her left side with left rib fractures → splenic laceration. 439
  • Blunt trauma, stable, FAST positive → CT with contrast 442; stable penetrating trauma → CT with IV contrast 441; responded to fluids, RUQ and chest tenderness → CT abdomen. 438 ×3
  • Child hit by the handlebar, pain and can't eat → duodenum 439; 10-year-old with a duodenal haematoma, stable → NPO + NG decompression. 442
Notes

Solid-Organ Injury

Important solid organs in abdominal trauma: spleen, liver, kidneys — these can produce major internal hemorrhage.

Notes

Splenic Injury

The spleen is fragile and one of the common sources of intra-abdominal hemorrhage after trauma.

Presentation: abdominal pain, LUQ/left flank tenderness, left shoulder referred pain (Kehr sign), features of hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock if bleeding is significant.

ModalityRole
FASTDetects free intra-abdominal fluid/blood; cannot precisely grade or always prove the spleen is the source, but in the appropriate trauma context free intraperitoneal blood raises suspicion of splenic injury
CTStable patient → CT for organ identification, laceration, grading, and active bleeding
SPLENIC INJURY GRADING
Graded I–V; increasing grade = increasing severity. Grade I: small subcapsular hematoma and laceration <1 cm. Higher grades involve progressively deeper laceration, larger hematoma, vascular involvement, or major splenic disruption.

Management — Main Determinant = Hemodynamic Stability

StatusManagement

Management of the Injured Patient

Trauma is one of the most significant public health concerns in the United States and worldwide. It is the leading cause of death among people aged 1-45 and results in more lost working years than any other cause of mortality.

I. Epidemiology of Trauma
Leading cause of death in young individuals (1-45 years old)

Major contributor to elderly hospitalizations (6% of Medicare admissions) Alcohol involvement: One-third of traffic-related deaths Economic burden: Estimated cost $671 billion annually

II. Trauma Death Distribution: The Evolution from Trimodal to Bimodal

Traditionally, trauma deaths followed a trimodal distribution, but due to advancements in trauma systems, this pattern has shifted to a bimodal distribution.

A. Immediate Deaths (Seconds to Minutes)
  • Occurs at the scene of injury → Patients die before reaching the hospital.
  • Causes:
  • Massive brain or spinal cord trauma
  • Exsanguination (massive hemorrhage)
  • Survival chances: Extremely low, even with immediate care.
  • Prevention is the key strategy (e.g., seat belts, helmets, firearm control).
B. Early Deaths (Minutes to a Few Hours)
  • Occur within the first few hours post-injury.
  • 50% due to internal hemorrhage, 50% due to CNS injuries.
  • Potentially treatable with rapid intervention.
  • Key strategies to reduce mortality:
  • Rapid transport (e.g., air ambulance, trauma teams)
  • Trauma centers with immediate surgical capability
  • Early hemorrhage control (e.g., damage control resuscitation, permissive hypotension, TXA administration)
  • Advanced neurocritical care for traumatic brain injury (TBI)
C. Late Deaths (Days to Weeks)
  • Historically associated with multiple organ failure (MOF) and sepsis.
  • Now predominantly caused by refractory intracranial hypertension.
  • Key strategies for reduction:
  • Aggressive critical care (e.g., sepsis prevention, early mobility, nutritional support)
  • Advancements in neurocritical care
  • Improved infection control measures
III. Trauma Systems & Improved Outcomes
Trauma centers provide:
  • 24/7 rapid resuscitation and operating room access
  • Protocol-driven care (Advanced Trauma Life Support - ATLS)
  • Specialized teams (trauma surgeons, critical care physicians, anesthesiologists, neurosurgeons, orthopedic surgeons)

The goal of a trauma system is to minimize preventable morbidity and mortality by ensuring that injured patients receive timely, organized, and efficient care. A well-structured trauma system includes prehospital triage, rapid transport, definitive care, and rehabilitation.

Key Components of a Trauma System
  • Prehospital Care: Identification, triage, treatment, and transportation of trauma patients.
  • Trauma Triage Protocols: Standardized anatomic and physiologic criteria to identify critically injured patients.
  • Regional Trauma Centers: Coordination with EMS providers for seamless transfer and care.
  • Disaster Preparedness: Trauma centers are equipped to manage mass casualty incidents.
II. Levels of Trauma Centers (American College of Surgeons Designation)

The American College of Surgeons (ACS) classifies trauma centers into four levels, depending on capabilities and resources.

Level IThe highest level of trauma care with 24/7 availability of trauma
surgeons, neurosurgeons, orthopedic surgeons, plastic surgeons,
anesthesiologists, and radiologists. Includes teaching and research
obligations.
Level IIProvides comprehensive trauma care but may lack some specialized services and research/education programs.
Level IIIFocuses on initial assessment, resuscitation, and stabilization,
followed by surgical treatment or transfer to a higher-level trauma
center.
Level IVOffers Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) and stabilization before transferring patients to a higher-level center. Primarily found in rural and remote areas.
III. Trauma Triage & Field Triage Guidelines

Triage Criteria (CDC Guidelines):

1- Vital Signs & Level of Consciousness

  • Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) ≤ 13
  • Systolic Blood Pressure < 90 mmHg
  • Respiratory Rate < 10 or > 29 breaths/min
2- Anatomic Criteria (Serious Injuries Requiring Trauma Center Care)
  • Penetrating injuries to head, neck, torso, or extremities
  • Chest wall instability or deformity (flail chest)
  • Two or more long-bone fractures
  • Crushed, degloved, or mangled extremity
  • Pelvic fractures
  • Open or depressed skull fractures
3- Mechanism of Injury & Energy Transfer
  • Falls > 20 feet (adults) or > 10 feet (children)
  • High-speed motor vehicle crashes (> 40 mph)
  • Vehicle ejection, rollover, or intrusion > 12 inches
  • Pedestrian or bicyclist struck by vehicle at > 20 mph
  • Motorcycle crash > 20 mph

Prehospital Care & Immediate Measures at an Incident Site I. Initial Response to Trauma at the Scene Trauma victims may not always exhibit visible external injuries, but a high-impact mechanism of injury should raise suspicion for severe internal trauma. The initial management priorities at the scene follow a structured approach to prevent further injury and stabilize the patient for transport.

Key Immediate Actions at the Scene

1- Assess Airway & Breathing

  • Ensure the victim is breathing.
  • If not, provide an airway (jaw thrust or chin lift) and establish bag-mask ventilation.
2- Check Circulation
  • If there is no pulse, begin closed-chest compressions (CPR).
3- Control Major Bleeding
  • Apply direct pressure and elevate the limb if possible.
  • Use a tourniquet for severe extremity bleeding (recommended for trained personnel).
4- Protect the Spine & Neck
  • Assume a cervical spine injury if the mechanism of trauma is significant.
  • Immobilize the neck and spine before moving the patient.
5- Splint Obvious Fractures
  • Stabilize any fractures or suspected dislocations before transport.
6- Prepare for Safe Transport
  • Once stabilized, transport the patient to a trauma center as quickly as possible.
STOP THE BLEED Initiative
  • Created after the Sandy Hook shooting in 2012 to teach civilians bleeding control techniques.
  • Public education on hemorrhage control (tourniquets, wound packing, direct pressure) can save lives.
II. Trauma Patient Evaluation & ATLS Approach

In most situations, prehospital personnel provide critical history via radio or when handing over the patient. Mechanism of injury (MOI) can provide clues to concealed trauma and help guide the trauma team’s assessment.

  • Important Prehospital Information
  • Motor Vehicle Collisions (MVCs): Speed, seatbelt use, airbag deployment,
  • ejection, and condition of passengers.
  • Fall or Crush Injuries: Height of fall, surface landed on, and time since
  • injury.
  • Penetrating Trauma: Type of weapon, number of wounds, distance from
  • the shooter, and exit wounds.
  • Medical Conditions: Medic Alert bracelets or history of anticoagulant use.

Shock in Trauma Patients

Shock is defined as inadequate end-organ tissue perfusion, which can rapidly lead to multi-organ failure and death if not treated promptly.

Types of Shock in Trauma & Their Management
A. Hypovolemic Shock (Most Common in Trauma)
  • Cause: Blood loss from hemorrhage (internal or external), major fractures,
  • burns, or severe crush injuries.
  • Signs: Pallor, cool skin, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypotension, oliguria,
  • altered mental status, acidosis.
Classification of Hemorrhagic Shock

Management of Hypovolemic Shock 1. Secure Two Large-Bore IV Lines (14-16G) or IO Access 2. Fluid Resuscitation Strategy:

  • Crystalloids (Ringer’s lactate/NS) 1-2 L bolus first
  • If no response after 1.5L, initiate massive transfusion protocol (MTP)

3. Blood Transfusion Guidelines:

  • ≥ Class III Shock → Start O-negative or type-specific PRBCs
  • 1:1:1 ratio of PRBC: FFP: Platelets (guided by TEG/ROTEM)
  • Goal: MAP ≥ 65 mmHg, Urine output ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/hr

4. Monitor for Lactic Acidosis & Coagulopathy

  • Check ABG, lactate, base deficit (metabolic acidosis = under- resuscitation)
  • Prevent the Lethal Triad (Hypothermia, Acidosis, Coagulopathy)

5. Definitive Hemorrhage Control:

  • Surgery or Angioembolization for internal bleeding
  • Tourniquets for extremity hemorrhage
B. Neurogenic Shock
  • Cause: Spinal cord injury (above T6) causing sympathetic tone loss, leading
  • to massive vasodilation and pooling of blood.
  • Signs: Warm, flushed skin, hypotension, bradycardia, preserved urine
  • output.
Management of Neurogenic Shock

1. IV Fluid Bolus → 2L of crystalloid first 2. If unresponsive, initiate Vasopressor Therapy:

  • Phenylephrine (first-line) → Pure α-agonist, restores vascular tone
  • Norepinephrine (if BP remains low)

3. Spinal Precautions:

  • Cervical spine immobilization
  • MRI & neurosurgery consultation
C. Cardiac Compressive (Obstructive) Shock

Cause: External compression of the heart leading to decreased venous return and cardiac output.

  • Common in Trauma: Pericardial tamponade, Tension pneumothorax, Diaphragmatic rupture.
  • Signs: Beck’s Triad → Hypotension + JVD + Muffled heart sounds
  • Pulsus paradoxus (SBP drops >10mmHg during inspiration)
Management of Cardiac Tamponade

1. Perform Emergency Pericardiocentesis (16 gauge) (U/S-guided) 2. Definitive: Pericardial Window or Thoracotomy in OR

Management of Tension Pneumothorax

1. Immediate Needle Decompression (2nd ICS, midclavicular line) 2. Definitive: Chest Tube Placement (5th ICS, midaxillary line)

D. Cardiogenic Shock
Cause: Decreased myocardial contractility from:
  • Blunt cardiac trauma (Myocardial contusion)
  • MI due to pre-existing CAD in older patients
  • Arrhythmias from electrolyte disturbances or hypoxia

Signs: Hypotension, pulmonary edema, JVD, weak pulse, cool skin.

Management of Cardiogenic Shock

1. Fluids (Small boluses) → Do NOT overload 2. Echocardiography to assess function 3. Inotropes: Dobutamine or Milrinone 4. Mechanical support (ECMO or IABP) in severe cases

1. Ensure Airway & Breathing (Oxygenation)

3. Early Recognition of Head Trauma

  • If decreasing GCS → Urgent head CT to assess for:
    • Epidural hematoma (rapid deterioration)
    • Subdural hematoma (common in elderly)

  • Cerebral injuries: Extradural/subdural hemorrhage → Urgent decompression.
  • Massive intra-abdominal bleeding → Immediate laparotomy.
  • Penetrating chest trauma with cardiac tamponade → Emergency thoracotomy.

5. Definitive Fracture Management

  • Long bone fractures → Urgent external fixation or traction.
  • Open fractures → Irrigation, debridement, antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis.
  • Pelvic fractures → Pelvic binder, embolization if bleeding.

6. Preventing the Lethal Triad in Trauma:

  • Acidosis → pH <7.2 worsens metabolic failure.
  • Coagulopathy → INR >1.5, prolonged PT/PTT, low platelets.

  • Prevent hypothermia: Warm IV fluids, blankets, room temp control.
  • Correct acidosis: Early blood transfusions, avoid excessive crystalloids.
  • Manage coagulopathy: Early plasma, platelets, and fibrinogen.

2. Resuscitation in ICU

  • Restore normal coagulation, perfusion, & body temperature.

3. Definitive Surgery (24-48 hours later)

  • Definitive bowel anastomosis, vascular grafts, abdominal closure.

Thoracic trauma contributes to 50% of trauma-related deaths due to its impact on airway, circulation, and respiratory function. Rapid identification and management of life-threatening conditions are crucial.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure and assess for tracheal injury, obstruction, or tension pneumothorax.
  • Breathing: Look for flail chest, pneumothorax, hemothorax, or pulmonary contusion.
  • Circulation: Identify cardiac tamponade, aortic injury, or massive hemorrhage.
  • Disability (Neurologic): Monitor for spinal cord injury or hypoxia-induced brain dysfunction.
  • Exposure: Examine for penetrating wounds, bruising, subcutaneous emphysema.
Life-Threatening Thoracic Injuries (The “Deadly Six”):

1. Airway obstruction 2. Tension pneumothorax 3. Massive hemothorax 4. Flail chest 5. Open pneumothorax 6. Cardiac tamponade

Abdominal Trauma:

Abdominal trauma is categorized into penetrating and blunt injuries. Early identification and appropriate intervention are key to preventing shock, sepsis, and multiorgan failure.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)

  • Circulation: Assess for hemorrhagic shock, a leading cause of death.
  • Disability (Neurologic): Identify signs of shock or brain injury.
  • Exposure: Check for seatbelt signs, bruising, penetrating wounds.

Vascular Trauma:

Vascular injuries pose a high risk of mortality and limb loss if not rapidly diagnosed and treated. Early identification and intervention are crucial to prevent exsanguination, ischemia, and complications like compartment syndrome.

Initial Assessment: Primary Survey (ABCDE)
  • Airway: Secure airway if unstable.
  • Breathing: Identify associated thoracic injuries.
  • Circulation: Stop bleeding immediately (direct pressure, tourniquet if needed).
  • Disability (Neurologic): Check for neurologic deficits (suggest ischemia or embolism).
  • Exposure: Identify all injury sites.
Key Red Flags for Vascular Injury:
  • Active pulsatile bleeding
  • Expanding hematoma
  • Absent or diminished pulses
  • Cold, pale, or cyanotic limb
  • Severe pain out of proportion to injury (suggests ischemia)
Types of Vascular Injuries
1- Penetrating Trauma
  • Causes: Gunshot wounds (GSWs), stab wounds, iatrogenic catheter injuries.
  • Complications: Hemorrhage, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula (AVF).
Gunshot Wounds
  • High kinetic energy → severe tissue damage
  • More likely to cause thrombosis and embolism
  • Require imaging (arteriography or CT angiogram)
Stab Wounds
  • Lower risk of vascular injury unless deeply penetrating
  • Doppler ultrasound or angiography if vascular injury suspected
2- Blunt Trauma
  • Causes: Motor vehicle crashes, falls, crush injuries, orthopedic trauma.
  • Common Sites:
  • Thoracic aorta (high-speed crashes, deceleration injuries)
  • Popliteal artery (posterior knee dislocation)
  • Carotid & vertebral arteries (neck trauma, C-spine fractures)
Blunt Thoracic Aortic Injury (BTAI):
  • High mortality (57% die before hospital arrival)
  • Common site: Aortic isthmus (just distal to left subclavian artery)
  • Diagnosis: CT angiography of the chest
  • Management:
  • Stable: Endovascular stent graft preferred
  • Unstable: Open thoracotomy

  • Caused by reperfusion after prolonged ischemia

  • Pallor

  • Delayed revascularization (>6 hrs)
  • Severe swelling post-repair
2- Amputation Criteria
Immediate Amputation:
  • Nonviable limb (prolonged ischemia, necrosis)
  • Severe crush injury with mangled extremity
  • Sepsis from uncontrolled infection
  • No reconstructable vascular flow
Delayed Amputation:
  • Failed revascularization
  • Severe neuropathy with no functional recovery
  • Uncontrolled pain or infection
